# Definition of creativity

## The standard definition

Runco and Jaeger (2012) reviewed the history of definitions of creativity and labelled the shared core the "standard definition". In their words (Runco & Jaeger, 2012, p. 92, as quoted in Abraham, 2025): "The standard definition is bipartite: Creativity requires both originality and effectiveness."

1. **Originality**: also called novelty, uniqueness, newness or unusualness (Abraham, 2025).
2. **Effectiveness**: also called usefulness, value, adaptiveness, fit or appropriateness (Abraham, 2025).

Both components are required together (Runco & Jaeger, 2012). Originality alone is not enough, because rare responses that stem from ignorance, randomness or delusion could otherwise be mistaken for originality (Barron, 1955, as cited in Abraham, 2025).

The definition has been used tacitly since at least the 1950s. Its earliest formulation is attributed to Morris Stein (Runco & Jaeger, 2012, as summarised in Abraham, 2025). Stein (1953) wrote: "The creative work is a novel work that is accepted as tenable or useful or satisfying" (quoted in Abraham, 2025).

## Variants

- Many definitions use the same two-part structure with different wording. Plucker et al. (2004, p. 90) define creativity as a product that is "both novel and useful as defined within a social context" (quoted in Abraham, 2025).
- **Adding surprise as a third criterion.** Boden defines a creative idea as novel, valuable and surprising (Boden, 2004, as summarised in Abraham, 2025). See [[boden-three-types]]. Simonton (2012) bases a three-criterion definition on the criteria the US Patent Office uses to evaluate patent applications: novelty, utility and surprise. He treats creativity ratings on these criteria as quantitative and multiplicative rather than additive.
- **Refining the criteria.** Corazza (2016) proposes a dynamic definition based on *potential* originality and effectiveness. Abraham (2025) proposes that a creative idea is one that is "both novel and satisfying".

## Criticisms

- **"Effectiveness" is loose.** Boden (2009) notes that "valuable" can mean interesting, useful, beautiful, simple, richly complex and more. Abraham (2025) reviews the philosophical and practical problems of operationalising value, including the fact that it depends on context. See [[domains-of-creativity]].
- **Originality is relative.** Stein (1953) already distinguished between internal and external frames of reference (quoted in Abraham, 2025). A child who fixes a tricycle bell for the first time may go through a process structurally similar to that of a genius, even though the product is not new to the world. Boden's P/H distinction and the [[four-c-model]] address the same question.
- **Bias toward the recipient's judgment.** The standard definition is usually applied from an external frame of reference, meaning the judgment of the people receiving the idea. The creator's internal frame of reference is ignored, and Abraham (2025) argues that this limits what research on the creative process can conclude.
- **"Effective" does not mean benevolent.** People who intend harm can also show creativity. Cropley et al. (2008) call this malevolent creativity and argue that it follows the same principles as benevolent creativity, differing only in its intended purpose. See [[dark-side-of-creativity]].

## Who judges?

The definition says what creativity is, but not who decides. In practice the judgment is usually made by the recipients of an idea (Abraham, 2025), and some definitions build the social context in explicitly (Plucker et al., 2004). See [[confluence-theories]] and the "audience" in [[four-ps-and-five-as]].
